Phase two hooks into the e-service email inbox so every incoming filing is screened automatically.
ideas.why_now: The volume of fabricated-citation filings is now measured in the thousands and judges have seen enough to act on them. Open case-law data (CourtListener) is now good enough that OpenAI built Astra for Law on it (17 Sep 2026), so the verification corpus is cheap for a small team.
ideas.revenue_model: $49-149 per filing report self-serve, or $1,500-5,000/month flat for repeat defendants with inbox integration. Upsell is drafting of the sanctions or strike motion at a fixed fee.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The buyer everyone targets (the erring lawyer) has a small budget and an embarrassment problem. The money and standing sit with the counterparty, who pays hourly to verify someone else's junk and is the only actor who can turn a bad cite into leverage (strike, fee-shifting, vexatious-litigant designation).
ideas.first_30_days: Build on eyecite and the CourtListener API, then benchmark accuracy on 100 known cases from the Charlotin database as ground truth. Cold-email 30 landlord-tenant and employment-defense firms and 10 municipal risk pools, offering 10 free reports in exchange for permission to attach a report to a filing. Charge $99 per report after that and aim for 3-5 recurring accounts.

ideas.title: Court-Rules MCP Server With a Deadline Warranty
ideas.one_liner: Effective-dated, human-verified court rules, judge standing orders and deadline math for one state at a time, exposed to any AI agent, with fee credits if a computed deadline is wrong.
ideas.customer: Solo and small firms (5 or fewer attorneys) in personal injury, family, criminal defense and landlord-tenant who already run Clio or MyCase and are starting to use Claude or ChatGPT agents. Later, legal-AI vendors that buy the rule set by API.
ideas.problem: Missed deadlines are among the most common malpractice claims (background knowledge, verify). General models know case law roughly but not this county's local rules, this judge's standing order (including AI-use certifications), or this year's fee schedule. The rules live as PDFs across thousands of court sites and change constantly, and big-firm docketing systems are priced and built for large firms.
ideas.solution: Start with one state pack, for example Texas civil. It holds statutes of limitation, civil procedure, local rules of the top counties and judge standing orders, each effective-dated with a hashed source PDF. MCP tools such as compute_deadline(event, court, date) and check_filing(court, judge, doc_type) return the date, the rule cites and a confidence flag. A deterministic engine does the date math (no LLM arithmetic), paid legal editors verify the high-use rules, and change alerts go out. A small warranty (fee credit plus capped reimbursement) backs the deadline output.
ideas.why_now: 8am's MyCase says 60+ firms, mostly 5 or fewer attorneys, adopted its Claude MCP connector (73 actions) in the first month, so small firms are now consuming practice tools through agents. Case law is open and the model is free, but local procedure is not in any frontier legal product.
ideas.revenue_model: $79-149/month per firm per state pack, an API license of $2-10k/month for legal-AI vendors, and a premium warranty tier.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: When the model is free and the corpus is open, the scarce asset is authoritative, effective-dated local procedure with a liability wrapper. Nobody can warrant an LLM's legal reasoning, but a rules engine plus editorial verification is exactly where a warranty is underwritable.
ideas.first_30_days: Pick one state and one practice area. Hand-build the 300 highest-frequency rules with two contract paralegals (about $8-10k), ship a free MCP server, and recruit 15 firms through a state solo and small-firm bar list. Charge $99/month after the trial, publish an accuracy audit, and keep the warranty to a $500 credit until loss data exists.

ideas.title: CRA Technical-File Compiler Built Into CI
ideas.one_liner: A GitHub/GitLab app that assembles the Cyber Resilience Act technical documentation, Annex I evidence and draft declaration of conformity from every release, so compliance is a build artifact rather than a consulting project.
ideas.customer: Product-security leads and CTOs at connected-device makers with 20-300 engineers (smart home, industrial IoT, e-bikes, wearables, network gear, EV chargers) selling into the EU. Not the GRC team.
ideas.problem: CRA reporting duties began 11 Sep 2026, full application is 11 Dec 2027, and fines reach EUR 15M or 2.5% of turnover. Manufacturers must keep versioned technical documentation (risk assessment, design, vulnerability handling, test evidence, SBOM), for roughly ten years or the support period. GRC platforms produce policy evidence, SBOM tools produce component lists, and consultants charge tens of thousands per product line for a file that goes stale on the next release.
ideas.solution: The app reads the repo, CI logs, SBOM (SPDX/CycloneDX), threat-model files and test results, then maps them to the Annex I essential requirements and vulnerability-handling duties. It posts gaps as pull-request comments ('no secure-update mechanism documented'). Each release yields a signed, timestamped technical-file bundle (PDF plus machine-readable), a declaration-of-conformity draft, a support-period statement and a diff from the previous release.
ideas.why_now: Reporting is already live and full application is 15 months away, so products in design today are locking in the choices that determine compliance cost. Harmonised standards are still arriving, so teams need structured evidence now rather than a finished standard to tick off.
ideas.revenue_model: SaaS at $1,500-6,000/month per product line, EUR 5-15k onboarding, and referral revenue from test labs and notified bodies.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Insiders assume Vanta/Drata-style GRC platforms will absorb the CRA. But the CRA is product regulation: the evidence lives in Git, CI and design docs and must be regenerated each release. That is a developer-tool, bottom-up sale to engineers, not a compliance-officer sale.
ideas.first_30_days: Interview 15 device makers via CRA meetups and open-source foundations working on CRA. Build a CLI that ingests a CycloneDX SBOM plus a small cra.yaml and emits a skeleton technical file. Run three paid pilots (EUR 3-5k) that produce each firm's first file, and publish the Annex I checklist as open source to draw inbound.

ideas.title: Regulatory Slip Desk for Compliance Budget Decisions
ideas.one_liner: A probability-weighted deadline desk that tells compliance heads which rules will probably slip, which will not, and which controls are worth building now regardless.
ideas.customer: GCs, heads of compliance and CFOs at companies with $200M-$20B revenue facing many regimes at once (EU AI Act, CBAM, CRA, CSRD, US state privacy and AI laws). Secondary buyers are compliance-software vendors timing their sales and investors betting on delay.
ideas.problem: Deadlines have become unreliable. AI Act high-risk duties moved to 2 Dec 2027 (Annex III) and 2 Aug 2028 (Annex I) per the tracker (the Omnibus status is unverified), CSRD waves 2 and 3 slipped to 2028, while CBAM and CRA reporting did not move. Teams either overspend on rules that later slip or get blindsided by rules that hold. Law-firm alerts explain what a rule says, not whether it will arrive on time.
ideas.solution: A subscription tracker of about 100 obligations, each with the hard date, a written probability of further slip or scope cut with reasons (trilogue calendar, standards readiness, member-state transposition, litigation), and a split between 'no-regret controls' that satisfy several regimes (inventories, logging, supplier data) and 'wait for clarity' items. Trigger alerts ('if standard X is not cited by date Y, slip probability rises'). A public scored track record of every past forecast, plus a quarterly board memo.
ideas.why_now: 2025-26 was the year of delays and unwinds: the Digital Omnibus reshuffled AI Act dates, CSRD got stop-the-clock, and several US rules were dropped or vacated (background, verify). Buyers have now been burned in both directions.
ideas.revenue_model: $12-40k/year per enterprise seat pack, a $3k/year SME tier sold via newsletter, and a data feed to compliance-software vendors at $30-100k.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Compliance is an options problem, not a deadline problem. Insiders sell obligations as fixed; the value is pricing probability and timing and finding multi-regime no-regret work. A public forecast track record is a moat law firms will not build because they cannot afford to be visibly wrong.
ideas.first_30_days: Publish a free 'Slip Index' showing the base rate of deadline moves across the 30 largest EU and US digital rules since 2023. Build a 500-person newsletter via IAPP-style and LinkedIn communities, and pre-sell 10 annual subscriptions at a $6k founder price with a money-back guarantee. Make every forecast in writing with a date.

ideas.title: PFAS Test-Result Exchange for Small Brands
ideas.one_liner: A members' data pool where small brands share lab results indexed by supplier, material lot and SKU, so nobody pays $500+ to test the same fabric or coating twice.
ideas.customer: Product-compliance managers at small and mid-size apparel, outdoor, cookware, cosmetics, textile and food-packaging brands and importers ($5M-$200M revenue) selling into US states with PFAS product laws and into the EU.
ideas.problem: PFAS rules are fragmenting through state product bans and reporting laws, EU packaging limits and a pending EU universal restriction (all unverified in the briefing; re-check current status). Supplier declarations fail because suppliers often do not know what is in their coatings. Testing costs hundreds of dollars per sample, and small brands that buy from the same mills and coaters each test alone. 'PFAS-free' marketing claims also draw class actions.
ideas.solution: A neutral cooperative. Members upload lab PDFs, which are parsed automatically and tagged to supplier, mill, material spec and date. The exchange scores confidence per supplier-material ('3 independent labs, 12 samples, all under threshold'), flags outliers, recommends where a new test buys the most certainty per dollar, negotiates group lab rates, and generates the state or EU evidence file. Contributions earn credits.
ideas.why_now: State PFAS product deadlines and EU packaging PFAS limits are landing in 2025-26 (background, verify), total-fluorine screening is cheap enough to run routinely, and LLM parsing turns messy lab PDFs into structured data.
ideas.revenue_model: Membership of $3-15k/year by revenue tier, pay-per-query for non-contributors, a 10-15% margin on group lab testing, and a paid 'independently verified' badge program.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Declarations fail through ignorance, not malice, so the durable defense is measurement. Measurement is a shared-cost, non-competitive good, like a credit bureau for materials. Antitrust risk is low if the pool holds test data only and never pricing.
ideas.first_30_days: Partner with one accredited lab and one trade association (outdoor or apparel). Recruit 10 founding members who contribute 200+ historical lab reports, stand up a spreadsheet-backed MVP with parsed PDFs, and charge a $2.5k founding fee.

ideas.title: Guardrail Gateway for Law-Firm AI Agents
ideas.one_liner: A policy proxy between AI agents and practice-management, billing and trust-accounting systems that enforces ethics rules (trust funds, conflicts, confidentiality) and logs every action for the bar and the insurer.
ideas.customer: Solo and small firms (5 or fewer attorneys), the exact segment adopting MCP connectors. Distribution partners are practice-management vendors and malpractice carriers that want to underwrite agent use.
ideas.problem: 8am's MyCase MCP connector exposes 73 actions across cases, billing and intake, and 60+ firms adopted it in month one. An agent that can write to billing and trust ledgers can commingle funds, send a privileged detail to the wrong client or email a client without review. Those are disciplinary and malpractice events that no hallucination checker prevents, and solo lawyers have no IT staff, policy or audit trail.
ideas.solution: An MCP gateway between Claude, ChatGPT or a 'Firm Agent' and Clio, MyCase and LawPay. Rules block any write touching the trust account without attorney approval by SMS, enforce ethical walls between matters, redact privileged content going to non-approved models, hold outbound client communications for review and rate-limit actions. Every call goes into a tamper-evident log, and a monthly 'agent audit' PDF answers the insurer questionnaire.
ideas.why_now: 8am launched its MCP integration in Sep 2026 and says nearly all of its new Firm Agent features already work via MCP, so law-practice data is flowing to third-party agents for the first time. ABA Formal Opinion 512 (2024) on generative-AI ethics gives the duties a written source (background, verify).
ideas.revenue_model: $79-199/firm/month, carrier-sponsored programs at $10-20 per insured firm per month, and white-label licensing to practice-management vendors.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The risk from agents is authority (moving money and information), not wrong words. Legal ethics rules are crisp about authority (trust accounting, confidentiality, conflicts), so they compile into policy, unlike 'accuracy'. Distribution will run through practice-management marketplaces, not law-firm websites.
ideas.first_30_days: Build the gateway for one platform (Clio or MyCase MCP) with six rules. Recruit 10 small firms through user groups and run it free as a 30-day 'agent audit' that shows near-misses, then convert at $99/month. Take the audit output to two state-bar-affiliated malpractice carriers.

ideas.title: Data Act Access-Request Desk for Independent Repairers
ideas.one_liner: A clearinghouse that files, tracks and escalates EU Data Act data-access requests to connected-product makers on behalf of independent garages, installers and fleet operators.
ideas.customer: Independent repair-shop networks, heat-pump and solar installers, agricultural-machinery service firms and small fleet operators (10-500 vehicles or machines) in the EU, plus their trade associations.
ideas.problem: Connected products must give users direct data access by design from 12 Sep 2026, and users can direct sharing to third parties. Every manufacturer will build its own portal, format and terms, and has every incentive to slow-walk independents. The EU repair directive transposition deadline (31 Jul 2026) also just passed. Small firms know wrenches, not statutory request letters or how to reach a national competent authority.
ideas.solution: A standardized request generator, a directory of each manufacturer's access method, a tracker with statutory-timeline reminders, normalization of the most-wanted data (fault codes, usage, battery health) and an escalation pack for the national authority. Launch with five manufacturers in two product categories.
ideas.why_now: The Data Act design obligation date was 12 Sep 2026, the repair directive deadline was 31 Jul 2026 and the EU repair platform is due 1 Jan 2028. Independents just received rights with no plumbing.
ideas.revenue_model: $49-149/month per shop, $5-20 per vehicle or machine per year for fleets, association licenses, and paid negotiation of bulk access terms.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Compliance startups sell to the obligated party. The Data Act creates a beneficiary class that is fragmented and unsophisticated about law. The AirHelp pattern applies: rights that are costly to file individually but cheap to file collectively.
ideas.first_30_days: Sign two trade associations (independent aftermarket or agricultural repair). Send 20 manual requests across five OEMs and log response times, then publish an 'OEM Data Act responsiveness scorecard' to earn press and members. Charge $99/month.

ideas.title: Verifier-Ready Emissions Data Rooms for CBAM Exporters
ideas.one_liner: A metering-to-evidence pipeline that gives small non-EU steel, aluminum and fertilizer producers a clean, pre-audited data room for accredited verifiers, so their EU and UK buyers stop defaulting to punitive default values.
ideas.customer: Producers and processors with 50-500 employees in Turkey, India, Egypt, Vietnam, Ukraine and South Africa (steel re-rollers, extruders, wire and fastener makers, fertilizer blenders). Paid by the producer or subsidized by the EU/UK importer buying from them.
ideas.problem: CBAM entered its definitive phase in 2026 and UK CBAM starts 1 Jan 2027 across 8 sectors. Importers lacking actual emissions data fall back on default values, which carry a mark-up (background, verify). Accredited verifiers are scarce, and small producers keep energy invoices in spreadsheets with no monitoring plan, so verification is slow and expensive and importers cannot get usable data.
ideas.solution: A two-week onboarding: connect electricity and gas meters or invoices, production logs and precursor traceability, then generate the monitoring methodology plan, the emissions report in CBAM format and an evidence index. Internal pre-verification, hand-off to partner verifiers, quarterly refresh, and sharing of the verified data with each importer through an API.
ideas.why_now: The definitive period began in 2026, verification of 2026 imports lands in 2027, and UK CBAM begins in three months. Default-value cost pressure now exceeds the price of proper data collection.
ideas.revenue_model: EUR 6-25k/year per plant (producer-paid or importer-sponsored supplier program) plus a coordination fee per verification.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Everyone sells CBAM to the EU importer's finance team. The bottleneck is evidence-poor factories and verifier capacity upstream. Importers will fund supplier readiness because default values cost more than the tool, and verified plant data is reusable across every EU and UK customer of that plant.
ideas.first_30_days: Find three EU or UK importers of steel wire or fasteners with Turkish or Indian suppliers (trade fairs, LinkedIn) and offer a supplier-readiness pilot for five plants at EUR 3k each. Deliver with templates and spreadsheets and partner with one or two verifiers.

ideas.title: Documentation-Review Copilot for Notified Bodies and Labs
ideas.one_liner: Software that triages and pre-checks manufacturers' technical files for the third-party assessors that CRA, Machinery, radio-cyber and AI Act rules are about to swamp.
ideas.customer: EU notified bodies, cybersecurity and Common Criteria test labs and product-certification firms (10-500 staff), including newly designated ones.
ideas.problem: Third-party conformity assessment is required for higher-risk classes under several regimes: CRA important-Class II and critical products, the radio-equipment cyber delegated act, new Machinery Regulation duties from 20 Jan 2027, and AI Act biometrics (dates from background knowledge, verify). Assessor capacity is the bottleneck. Each file review takes weeks of expert time on incomplete, inconsistent submissions, and delay lands on the manufacturer's launch date.
ideas.solution: An intake portal that bounces incomplete submissions against a clause map, an LLM-assisted cross-check of claims versus test evidence versus SBOM, auto-generated clarification requests to the manufacturer, a reviewer workbench with evidence links, and traceable report drafting. EU-hosted or on-prem for confidentiality.
ideas.why_now: CRA reporting began 11 Sep 2026 and further obligations land 11 Dec 2027, while new-body designation and accreditation are slow. File volume is about to rise faster than assessor headcount.
ideas.revenue_model: $30-120k/year per lab, or per-reviewer seats at $500-1,500/month, plus implementation fees.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: In any permit regime the scarce resource is the assessor's hours, and manufacturers pay for delay. Selling to roughly 150 known assessors is easier than selling to 100,000 manufacturers, and it produces unique data on what a 'good file' looks like.
ideas.first_30_days: Email 40 labs and notified bodies and offer to pilot on a backlog of anonymized historical files. Run three paid pilots at EUR 5-10k, measure review-hours saved, and turn the results into a case study.

ideas.title: Opt-Out Time Machine for AI Training Compliance
ideas.one_liner: A historical archive of every site's machine-readable AI-training opt-outs (robots.txt, TDMRep, ai.txt, meta tags, headers) so model builders can prove what was reserved on the day they crawled.
ideas.customer: AI startups and labs that train or fine-tune on scraped or third-party data (especially EU-exposed), dataset publishers, and rights-holder groups (publishers, collecting societies) that need proof of their own reservations.
ideas.problem: GPAI obligations have applied since Aug 2025 and AI Office enforcement began in Aug 2026. Providers need a copyright policy and must respect machine-readable rights reservations under the EU text-and-data-mining exception (background, verify). Opt-out signals change over time and nobody retains neutral evidence of what a site said on a given day, yet disputes will turn on exactly that.
ideas.solution: A weekly crawl of the top ~50M domains capturing robots.txt, /.well-known/tdmrep.json, ai.txt, meta tags, headers and terms-page hashes, stored as signed, timestamped snapshots. API calls answer 'what did domain X reserve at time T?' and 'filter dataset D by reservations as of T'. Certificates of compliance for training corpora and monitoring alerts for rights holders whose reservations are ignored.
ideas.why_now: Enforcement powers over GPAI providers began Aug 2026, copyright-and-training cases are moving through European courts, and crawl and storage costs are low enough for a two-person team.
ideas.revenue_model: API subscriptions of $2-25k/month for labs and dataset teams, $5-30k per compliance certificate, and $500-5k/month for rights-holder monitoring.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Compliance evidence is a time-series problem. The neutral party that started archiving earlier owns the truth, and it cannot be recreated retroactively, so the moat begins accumulating on day one.
ideas.first_30_days: Crawl the top 1M domains weekly (a few hundred dollars a month) and publish a free opt-out prevalence report. Sign three EU AI startups or dataset publishers to paid pilots of $2-5k and approach one collecting society.

ideas.title: Outsourced 24-Hour Vulnerability Reporting Desk (CRA)
ideas.one_liner: A retainer service that acts as the manufacturer's PSIRT: it watches for actively exploited vulnerabilities in their products' components and files the 24-hour early warning, follow-up notification and final report to the EU platform.
ideas.customer: Connected-device makers with 20-500 employees selling into the EU with no 24/7 security team: smart home, e-bikes and scooters, industrial sensors, routers, wearables, toys, EV chargers. Many are non-EU (US and Asian) firms.
ideas.problem: CRA reporting obligations began 11 Sep 2026: 24-hour reporting to ENISA for actively exploited vulnerabilities and severe incidents, with fines up to EUR 15M or 2.5% of turnover. Small makers have no on-call rota, no SBOM monitoring and no idea what 'actively exploited' means for their firmware. The briefing found almost no visible tooling aimed at them.
ideas.solution: A retainer that ingests each product's SBOM per firmware version, matches it continuously against exploited-vulnerability and threat feeds, triages 24/7 with a pre-agreed decision tree, and files the early warning, notification and final report with text approved by the client's named contact. It also runs coordinated disclosure and advisory publishing, plus quarterly tabletop drills. Software lets one analyst cover 30+ clients.
ideas.why_now: The reporting duty went live 17 days ago and the full regime follows in Dec 2027. Firms are discovering that the deadline is a staffing problem, not a document problem.
ideas.revenue_model: EUR 1,500-6,000/month retainer, incident surcharges, and EUR 5k annual tabletop exercises.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: A 24-hour clock makes this a staffing obligation, which small firms cannot meet alone but a pooled desk can, like outsourced DPO services. Each reported vulnerability also gives a natural upsell into SBOM and technical-file work.
ideas.first_30_days: Partner with two or three EU security consultancies or product-safety associations. Sell a EUR 2.5k one-day 'CRA reporting readiness audit' to 20 firms, convert 5-8 into EUR 2k/month retainers, and contract three part-time analysts across time zones.

ideas.title: Repair-Rights Compliance Portal in a Box
ideas.one_liner: A hosted repair.yourbrand.com that publishes the parts lists, manuals, pricing and order forms that US state and EU repair laws require, plus the rules engine and audit trail behind it.
ideas.customer: Compliance, legal and customer-service leads at mid-market consumer-electronics, appliance, e-bike, power-tool and mobility brands ($30M-$1B revenue) selling in Washington, Texas, Oregon and the EU. Retailers are a second segment.
ideas.problem: Washington's law took effect 1 Jan 2026, Texas applies from Sep 2026 to electronics over $50, Oregon bans parts pairing, the EU directive's transposition deadline was 31 Jul 2026, and an EU repair platform is due 1 Jan 2028. Each regime differs in scope, dates and price rules, and the briefing found nobody selling compliance tooling for repair-information forms or parts-availability tracking.
ideas.solution: Portal templates and connectors: product-catalog import, SKU mapping to state or EU scope and effective dates, auto-published manuals and parts lists, a parts order form with a fair-price check, pairing-policy disclosures, an SLA timer and request log for regulators, and an EU repair-information-form generator. Regulatory updates ship as configuration changes.
ideas.why_now: Multiple obligations hit in the past nine months (Washington Jan 2026, EU transposition Jul 2026, Texas Sep 2026) and Oregon dates are still unclear in public sources, so brands cannot rely on a single law-firm memo.
ideas.revenue_model: $15-60k/year per brand by SKU count, $10-30k implementation, and a per-order fee on parts sales.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The core burden of repair law is publication and response time, which is CMS and workflow work, not legal analysis. Law firms bill hourly for what is really a web app, and the portal also cuts support costs.
ideas.first_30_days: Pick 30 mid-market brands with Texas exposure from product listings and email compliance leads a free one-page 'Texas gap audit'. Build a minimal portal for three design partners at a $5k pilot fee.

ideas.title: One Annual Fee for Every Mandatory EU Representative
ideas.one_liner: A roll-up of small EU authorised-representative shops that bundles every legally required local presence (GDPR Art. 27, AI Act, Data Act, product safety, CRA) into one liability-bearing annual contract for non-EU companies.
ideas.customer: US, UK, Israeli, Indian and Asian SaaS, AI and hardware companies ($2M-$200M revenue) selling in the EU without an EU entity. Bought by founders, GCs and ops leads.
ideas.problem: Several EU regimes require non-EU companies to name someone in the EU who can be held to account: GDPR Art. 27, AI Act authorised representatives for high-risk and GPAI providers, Data Act legal representative, product-safety responsible person, an optional CRA authorised representative (background knowledge; verify each). Today each comes from a different vendor, many are one-person shops or law firms wary of liability, and none coordinate.
ideas.solution: Acquire three to six small rep businesses (typically hundreds to a couple thousand clients on sticky annual fees), keep their brands, and rebuild operations with automation for inbound regulator and data-subject mail triage, translation and escalation. Add an EU law-firm panel as backstop and sell one bundle with a shared register of representations, one invoice and standard playbooks, priced for the liability.
ideas.why_now: GPAI duties applied Aug 2025 with enforcement from Aug 2026, Data Act obligations arrived Sep 2025 and Sep 2026, and CRA reporting started 11 Sep 2026, so many non-EU firms suddenly face three or four rep obligations at once. AI lowers the cost of delivering the service.
ideas.revenue_model: EUR 3-15k/year per client bundle, 70-80% renewal, acquisitions at roughly 1-2x revenue, and upsell to compliance retainers.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: When AI makes drafting free, the scarce good is someone in the EU who can be sued. Liability-bearing presence has pricing power and stickiness, and becoming the address regulators write to is a distribution moat.
ideas.first_30_days: List 30 small EU rep providers and approach five owners about a white-label or revenue-share deal that leads to acquisition. Sell the bundle to 10 US SaaS and AI firms through founder communities at EUR 4k and obtain a professional-indemnity quote.

ideas.title: Defensibility Desk for GenAI Document Review
ideas.one_liner: An independent validation service that samples, blind-reviews and documents the accuracy of AI-assisted document review so litigators can defend it to opposing counsel and judges.
ideas.customer: Litigation partners and e-discovery leads at mid-size firms (25-500 lawyers), corporate litigation departments, and ALSPs and e-discovery vendors moving first-pass review to LLMs.
ideas.problem: ALSPs are consolidating around AI-enabled workflows 'engineered around human review' (Repario acquired UnitedLex on 28 Sep 2026). Review has moved from TAR to LLM classification, and opposing parties and judges will ask for proof of recall and precision. Self-validation by the team that ran the review is neither independent nor consistent, and there is no accepted protocol for LLM review.
ideas.solution: A standard protocol: statistical sampling (elusion and recall estimates with confidence intervals), blind second-pass review by a bench of reviewers, adjudication of disagreements, drift checks across model versions, and a court-ready validation declaration with optional expert testimony. It plugs into Relativity, Everlaw and DISCO by API.
ideas.why_now: Generative-AI first-pass review went mainstream in 2025-26, private equity is rolling up ALSPs on the promise of AI plus human review, and judges are scrutinizing AI use in litigation.
ideas.revenue_model: $4-20k per matter validation, $60-250k/year programs for ALSPs, and hourly expert testimony.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: AI drives first-pass review cost toward zero, which makes independent validation the billable, defensible act, and independence is what gives it evidentiary weight (like an auditor). Displaced contract reviewers are a ready workforce for it.
ideas.first_30_days: Interview 15 e-discovery counsel and design the protocol with a statistician advisor. Run three pilot validations at $3-5k on closed matters and publish the protocol as a whitepaper to build credibility.

ideas.title: Battery Passport Onboarding for E-Bike and Storage Makers
ideas.one_liner: Done-for-you EU battery passport, QR labelling and supplier data collection for makers of e-bikes, scooters and industrial or stationary batteries facing the 18 Feb 2027 date.
ideas.customer: Mid-size e-bike, e-scooter and light-EV brands, industrial battery pack assemblers and BESS integrators selling in the EU (20-500 staff), plus importers who count as the manufacturer.
ideas.problem: The EU Battery Regulation requires from 18 Feb 2027 a QR code and electronic battery passport for EV, light-transport and industrial batteries above 2 kWh (background knowledge; verify current status and any slippage). The data spans composition, cell supplier, recycled content, carbon footprint and state of health, and it must be extracted from cell makers who resist sharing. Larger passport vendors serve automakers and big OEMs, so small assemblers fall through.
ideas.solution: A supplier data-collection portal with templates for cell makers, a passport record generator with public and restricted access tiers, QR label files, state-of-health data hooks, a compliance checklist and change updates, plus a service layer that chases suppliers until they answer.
ideas.why_now: About 20 weeks remain, delegated acts and standards are still in flux, and small makers cannot wait for perfect specs. Even if parts slip, buyers still need the underlying data.
ideas.revenue_model: EUR 8-30k onboarding plus EUR 3-10k/year platform per battery family, with supplier-chasing billed hourly.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The passport is a supplier-data-chasing problem, not a blockchain problem. Small buyers can pool leverage as a buying club so a cell maker answers one questionnaire instead of fifty.
ideas.first_30_days: Compile 200 EU e-bike and light-EV brands via a trade body and email a 'passport readiness scorecard'. Sign five design partners at EUR 5k and negotiate a template data sheet with two cell makers.

ideas.title: Notary for AI Agents' Authority to Sign
ideas.one_liner: A registry of signed, scoped, revocable 'mandates' that let a company's AI agents prove to counterparties what they may commit to, with a legal opinion and an insurer behind each.
ideas.customer: SMBs and mid-market firms deploying purchasing, AR/AP, sales-ops and scheduling agents (finance and ops leads), the fintech and AP-automation platforms embedding those agents, and the vendors on the receiving end.
ideas.problem: Agents now email vendors, accept quotes, change orders and click 'I agree'. Counterparties cannot tell whether an agent had authority, whose it is, or its spend limit, and companies cannot prove afterward what they authorized. Contract-formation doctrine (electronic-agent provisions, apparent authority) predates this. Payment protocols carry payment mandates, not authority to bind.
ideas.solution: Phase one: a legal template and JSON mandate schema (principal, agent identity, scope by category and counterparty, dollar cap, expiry, escalation), signed as verifiable credentials, with a public verify API and a revocation registry, an audit log, and a law-firm opinion letter on enforceability for the first US states. Any counterparty agent can call a check_mandate MCP tool. Phase two: an MGA-backed insurance product for agent commitments up to the mandate cap.
ideas.why_now: MCP and agent-payment protocols emerged in 2025 and small-firm agent adoption is visible now (60+ firms on MyCase's connector in one month), yet the contract-authority layer between payments and law has no owner (background, verify).
ideas.revenue_model: $50-500/month per business, per-verification fees for high-volume counterparties, an insurance premium share, and $10-25k enterprise opinion-letter packages.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Payment rails answer 'can this agent pay?' while the law asks 'was it authorized to bind?', and that depends on documented delegation, the same problem powers of attorney and corporate resolutions solved for humans. Whoever sets the schema counterparties check becomes the standard.
ideas.first_30_days: Draft the mandate schema and template with a partner law firm and publish an open spec. Pilot with five procurement or AP-agent startups, ship the verify API, get three design partners to put an authority header in agent emails, and open talks with two MGAs.

ideas.title: Conformity Cases for Learning-Enabled Robots
ideas.one_liner: A compliance workbench and pre-assessment service that builds the CE-marking safety case for machines whose behaviour comes from ML models (warehouse robots, cobots, humanoids) ahead of the new EU Machinery Regulation.
ideas.customer: CTOs and safety engineers at robotics startups and integrators (10-300 staff) selling autonomous mobile robots, cobot cells, agri-robots, humanoids and exoskeletons into the EU.
ideas.problem: The Machinery Regulation applies from 20 Jan 2027 and adds duties for machinery with self-evolving or learning behaviour and for cybersecurity (background, verify), with AI Act Annex I overlay dated 2 Aug 2028 in the tracker. Consultancies know ISO 12100 and 13849 but not how to argue the safety of a neural-network policy, notified bodies have no playbook, and startups cannot sell to EU customers without a CE dossier.
ideas.solution: Software plus an expert network: hazard-analysis templates for ML perception and control, runtime safety-monitor patterns (shielding, safe fallback, speed and separation monitoring), test evidence generated from simulation and field logs, and a traceable assurance case linking hazards to mitigations to evidence, mapped to Machinery, CRA and AI Act. A partner notified body does a pre-review.
ideas.why_now: Foundation-model-controlled and humanoid robots reached commercial pilots in 2025-26, and the regulatory dates arrive within months. Assurance-case methods from aviation and automated driving are mature but have not reached robotics.
ideas.revenue_model: EUR 25-80k per product safety-case project, $2-6k/month SaaS, and notified-body referral fees.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The blocker for deploying humanoids in Europe is not the model but an argument a regulator can accept. The first team whose safety cases are accepted creates precedent that competitors must copy, which is a durable moat.
ideas.first_30_days: Interview 20 robotics startups and publish an 'ML robot CE checklist'. Sign three design partners at EUR 10-15k for a gap analysis and recruit an ex-notified-body functional-safety engineer as co-founder or advisor.

ideas.title: Camera-to-Courtroom Evidence Provenance for Small Firms
ideas.one_liner: A capture app and export service that timestamps and cryptographically signs photos, video, texts and voicemails at collection, packaged with an authentication affidavit for court.
ideas.customer: Family-law, employment, landlord-tenant and personal-injury firms with up to 10 attorneys, their clients, legal-aid groups and HR investigators.
ideas.problem: Deepfakes make every screenshot and clip attackable. Courts and rule-makers are debating standards for machine-generated and possibly fabricated evidence (background, verify), and opposing counsel increasingly says 'that could be AI'. Honest clients then need a forensic expert at thousands of dollars per item to prove authenticity.
ideas.solution: Mobile capture that uses C2PA Content Credentials where phones support them (Pixel 10 added camera-level signing in 2025, background, verify) with a fallback for other devices, an SMS, WhatsApp and iMessage exporter with hash chaining, RFC 3161 trusted timestamps, chain-of-custody logs, and a one-click authentication package with a declaration template and a verifier page for the court. Optional expert-declaration add-on.
ideas.why_now: Mainstream phones gained hardware-backed provenance in 2025, judicial scrutiny of AI-generated evidence rose through 2025-26, and timestamping and signing infrastructure is now near-free.
ideas.revenue_model: $9-29 per case pack, $99-299/month per firm, and $250-500 per expert add-on.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The generative-AI problem for law is not only fake evidence getting in, but real evidence being dismissed. Provenance at creation is a right-of-reply tool for the party with fewer resources, so the customer is the weaker litigant's lawyer.
ideas.first_30_days: Ship the capture app and message exporter, pilot with 15 family-law solos, get a forensic examiner to co-sign the package and stage a mock authentication hearing with a law-school clinic. Charge $99/month afterward.

ideas.title: Federated Settlement-Benchmark Co-op for Small Firms
ideas.one_liner: Small plaintiff firms pool de-identified settlement outcomes from their practice-management systems to get case-value benchmarks that only insurers and big firms have today.
ideas.customer: Employment, wage-hour, personal-injury, med-mal and consumer boutiques with 1-15 attorneys. Later buyers are insurers, litigation funders and mediators purchasing aggregate indices.
ideas.problem: Verdict reporters capture only the few percent of cases that reach verdict, while nearly all money moves through confidential settlements. Insurers hold large claims databases, but plaintiff-side lawyers estimate value from gut feel and listservs. Frontier legal tools train on public opinions, not private outcomes, and outcome-priced legal work (as Norm Law sells) needs outcome data.
ideas.solution: With attorney approval, a practice-management connector extracts a handful of structured fields (claim type, venue, injury or violation class, damages band, procedural posture, time to resolution, fee outcome) into a secure aggregation layer with k-anonymity thresholds and differential privacy on outputs, no free text, and respect for confidentiality clauses. Members get instant valuation ranges and time-to-resolution, and aggregate indices are licensed to insurers and funders.
ideas.why_now: MCP connectors to practice-management systems are now real (8am: 60+ small firms in month one), privacy-preserving analytics tooling has matured, and outcome-based pricing plus a funded litigation-finance market create demand for outcome data.
ideas.revenue_model: Free for contributors (about 5 data points per quarter), $99-299/month for non-contributors, and $25-250k/year data licenses to insurers and funders.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The most valuable legal dataset is in no court file. It sits in hundreds of thousands of small-firm ledgers. Firms will trade aggregated outcomes for benchmarks (as doctors do for registries), and Westlaw cannot copy that give-to-get flywheel because it has no view into settlements. Rule 1.6 and settlement confidentiality clauses are the main risk and need an ethics memo up front.
ideas.first_30_days: Run it manually first. Recruit 20 employment or wage-hour lawyers through a state bar section or NELA chapter, collect 10 de-identified data points each on a form, return a valuation sheet, and commission an ethics counsel memo. Then build the connector for one platform.

ideas.title: Local-Law Radar for Data Center and Battery Developers
ideas.one_liner: A system that continuously reads city and county codes, planning agendas and minutes nationwide and warns developers which jurisdictions are drafting moratoria or new setback, noise and fire-safety rules before they pass.
ideas.customer: Land-acquisition and permitting teams at data-center, battery-storage, solar, EV-charging and peaker developers, siting consultants, and law-firm land-use groups.
ideas.problem: Local ordinances decide whether $100M-$1B projects get built, but roughly 19,000 municipalities publish codes and agendas as PDFs on inconsistent sites. Opposition-driven moratoria appear with weeks of notice, developers learn about them after buying land options, and existing zoning datasets capture setbacks and floor-area ratios, not conditional-use or moratorium rules for new infrastructure types.
ideas.solution: A scraper and LLM pipeline over municipal-code hosts and agenda platforms (Legistar, CivicClerk, PrimeGov and similar) that classifies items by project type, alerts on early signals ('first reading', 'study session', 'interim urgency ordinance'), answers 'is X permitted at parcel Y and under what conditions?', and scores county risk. Two land-use paralegals curate the output.
ideas.why_now: Data-center and battery-storage siting fights surged through 2025-26, including after the Jan 2025 Moss Landing battery fire (background, verify), and LLMs can now read messy municipal PDFs cheaply enough to cover thousands of jurisdictions.
ideas.revenue_model: $2-10k/month per developer team, $60-250k/year enterprise plans, and $500-2,000 per-parcel reports.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Moratoria are telegraphed weeks ahead in public agendas that nobody reads at scale, so the value is the leading indicator, not the code text. A stranded land option costs far more than the subscription.
ideas.first_30_days: Cover the three states with the most data-center activity and track about 500 jurisdictions' agendas. Publish a weekly free moratorium tracker, sell five developers or site-selection consultants at $2.5k/month, and back-test which past moratoria would have been flagged 30 days early.

ideas.title: Pay the Grandmother: Relative-Care Subsidy Enrollment
ideas.one_liner: A multilingual concierge plus verified-attendance software that turns unpaid grandparents and relatives into subsidy-paid, health-and-safety-cleared caregivers, billed per enrollment to states and referral agencies.
ideas.customer: State child-care subsidy (CCDF) lead agencies, county subsidy offices and child care resource and referral (CCR&R) agencies. Secondary: workforce boards and Head Start grantees.
ideas.problem: Deserts are measured in licensed slots (3+ kids per slot), but most parents actually cobble together relative care that the maps never count. Many states can already pay license-exempt relatives through subsidy. Families don't enroll because of fingerprinting, training, provider agreements and slow payment. States are also wary of fraud (federal subsidy-fraud scrutiny in winter 2025-26, from memory, not verified). So the 'supply' looks empty while grandmothers work for free.
ideas.solution: A guided onboarding flow in the caregiver's language covers document collection, fingerprint appointment booking, CPR and safe-sleep micro-training, and e-signed provider agreements. Attendance is logged by phone tap-in with geo-stamp and parent co-sign, which gives the state verified attendance. Payment goes out by direct deposit or prepaid card within days. A state dashboard shows 'real supply unlocked' by county.
ideas.why_now: Childcare costs hit about $13,128 a year (up 29% since 2020) while licensed supply barely grows (centers +1.5%, homes +4.3% in 2024). The 2024 federal CCDF rule (7% copay cap, enrollment-based prospective payment) is being implemented by states in 2025-26 (from memory). Universal-care promises (NYC per the brief) create demand for supply that needs no buildings. Fraud scrutiny makes verified attendance a selling point, not a cost.
ideas.revenue_model: Per completed enrollment fee ($150-400) plus a per-active-caregiver monthly fee ($3-8), paid by the agency under a pilot contract. Pilots run $30-60k per CCR&R or county.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The scarcest input in childcare deserts is not buildings or workers. It is unpaid supply that already exists, blocked by paperwork and by states' fear of fraud. The winner sells verified attendance as much as enrollment.
ideas.first_30_days: Pick two states with permissive relative-care rules. Map every enrollment step and drop-off point. Offer one CCR&R a free 25-family concierge pilot run over WhatsApp and phone, with Twilio and a no-code form behind it. Recruit through Spanish-, Somali- and Hmong-speaking community groups. Get a letter of intent from one county for a paid per-enrollment fee.

ideas.title: Youth Clubs as the Ban-Proof Group Chat
ideas.one_liner: A roster-anchored messaging layer for sports leagues, scout councils and youth groups that reuses the club's adult-verified roster as a safe, auditable chat for 9-15 year olds, paid by the club.
ideas.customer: Regional youth sports leagues, scout councils, robotics/FIRST teams and church youth groups (5k-100k members), plus their liability insurers. Parents use it free.
ideas.problem: Under-16 bans (Australia, Brazil, Indonesia, Malaysia, several US states) push kids into private chats and games. Everyone's answer is a new 'safe social network for kids', which dies on cold start. Meanwhile clubs already hold the verified network (background-checked coaches, rosters, parent contacts) but run it on WhatsApp, GroupMe and Snap groups with coach-to-child DMs. Youth-safety policies such as SafeSport's (from memory) prohibit exactly those DMs, and leagues cannot audit them.
ideas.solution: Team and league chats built on the registration data the club already has (DOB, parent identity). No one-to-one adult-minor DMs unless a second guardian is copied. Kid accounts are age-tiered and parent-linked, with no discovery, ads or strangers. Keyword flags go to the club safety officer. An exportable audit log goes to the insurer. Kids age out into open platforms at 16.
ideas.why_now: Ban leakage (VPNs under A$20 a month, 75% of Australian teens planning to stay on) means kids need somewhere else to talk. Insurers are tightening abuse-and-molestation coverage (from memory). Fall registration season is happening now, so the product can ride the season's registration fee.
ideas.revenue_model: $1-4 per member per season, bundled into the league's registration fee. Enterprise licence for councils. Referral fees or premium credits from insurers.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The hard part of safe kids' social is distribution and verification, not software. A club has the graph, the identity check, a legal duty of care and a budget, and nobody has packaged that.
ideas.first_30_days: Interview 15 league directors and two youth-sports insurers. Ship a white-label chat on Stream or Sendbird for two leagues in one metro. Sell it as 'audit-ready coach-athlete messaging' at $1 per kid during fall registration. Collect an insurer endorsement or premium-credit letter.

ideas.title: Independent Leakage Audits for Age Verification
ideas.one_liner: A red-team lab that measures how easily under-16s slip past each platform's age check (VPN, borrowed ID, face tricks) and sells defensible evidence to platforms, counsel and insurers.
ideas.customer: Mid-size social, gaming and video platforms operating in Australia, the UK, Brazil, Indonesia, Malaysia and US ban states. Also their outside counsel and, later, regulators.
ideas.problem: Insiders treat age assurance as a vendor-selection problem. Regulators judge whether 'reasonable steps' were taken. Australia is investigating five major platforms (fines up to A$49.5M) and proposed in June 2026 to double fines to about A$99M and reach app stores and age-assurance providers. By February 2026 many children had already bypassed the ban. Vendors self-report accuracy but nobody independently measures real-world leakage at the 14-17 border.
ideas.solution: A standard test harness of about 20 evasion scenarios (VPN region switch, parent's ID, older-sibling account, face-estimation edge cases, re-registration). It runs with consented adult testers and synthetic profiles, never with minors. Outputs are a quarterly public 'Leakage Index' plus confidential 'reasonable-steps evidence packs' and a continuous monitoring subscription.
ideas.why_now: Bans went live between December 2025 and June 2026 and enforcement is starting. The proposed extension of liability to age-assurance providers means everyone in the chain wants third-party evidence. The reported IDScan breach and Persona complaints (both from the brief, one flagged shaky) push platforms to question their vendors.
ideas.revenue_model: Confidential audits at $15-60k each. Monitoring subscription at $3-10k a month. Later, licensing the test protocol to regulators and insurers.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: This is an assurance market like SOC 2, not a technology market. The buyer wants a defensible paper trail, and it must be independent of the vendors it grades, so the lab should be paid by the platforms rather than the vendors.
ideas.first_30_days: Write the 20-scenario protocol with a regulatory lawyer. Run it on 5 public age gates in Australia using adult test accounts, keeping to what counsel clears. Publish a free 'Leakage Index' teaser. Cold-email trust-and-safety leads and regulatory counsel at 40 mid-size platforms with their own results.

ideas.title: Clinician-Prescribed AI Social Practice for Kids
ideas.one_liner: A bounded, transcript-visible role-play partner that speech-language pathologists prescribe to autistic and socially anxious kids, sold to districts that are legally obliged to deliver therapy minutes.
ideas.customer: School-district special-education departments, contract therapy staffing firms (SLP, psychology) and private pediatric therapy clinics.
ideas.problem: Insiders think kids plus AI is a no-go zone. Character.AI barred under-18s from open-ended chat in November 2025, and the FTC 6(b) inquiry and state laws (CA SB 243) followed. But districts must deliver IEP speech and social-communication minutes, SLP caseloads are huge and vacancies persist. Kids need many low-stakes repetitions between weekly 30-minute sessions.
ideas.solution: An anti-companion design: the SLP assigns scripted scenarios (ordering lunch, joining a game, handling teasing). There is no persona, no persistent memory and no free topics. Practice is recorded and the SLP dashboard produces the progress-monitoring data IEPs require. Parents can read transcripts. Voice-first, tuned for child speech, with no audio retention by default.
ideas.why_now: Regulators and lawsuits (Raine v. OpenAI, Pennsylvania v. Character.AI) closed the open-ended companion door, which makes scoped, clinician-in-the-loop tools the defensible lane. Speech models handle child speech far better than they did two years ago. Special-ed budgets are stretched (from memory).
ideas.revenue_model: Per-student annual licence ($150-400), much cheaper than added SLP hours at $60-100 an hour. Clinics pay per clinician seat.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The regulated lane isn't closed, it just has a different buyer: a clinician with a legal duty to document. Designing it as the opposite of a companion (no persona, no memory, no free chat) makes it compliant by construction and defensible in the next lawsuit.
ideas.first_30_days: Recruit 3 practicing SLPs to script 30 scenarios. Build a voice prototype. Run a 4-week paid pilot with about 10 kids in one private clinic ($99 a month per child). Then approach one contract-therapy staffing firm with the pilot's progress-monitoring data.

ideas.title: Ear-Coach for Early-Ed Teachers, Paid by QRIS
ideas.one_liner: Classroom-audio analysis that scores teacher-child interactions the way trained CLASS observers do and coaches staff weekly, sold to centers as a path to higher state quality-rating tiers and higher reimbursement.
ideas.customer: Directors and owners of centers and small chains (5-50 sites) in states with tiered-reimbursement QRIS programs. Also QRIS coaching contractors and Head Start grantees.
ideas.problem: Insiders picture AI in early education as child-facing. The real bottleneck is the adult: the average worker earns $33,140, turnover is high and coaching is sporadic. Quality-rating tiers drive subsidy-rate bonuses, but observation-based scoring needs scarce, costly trained observers, so centers stay stuck at low stars.
ideas.solution: Opt-in classroom audio pods or teacher-worn mics with on-device diarization and transcription (no child audio retained). They score serve-and-return turns, open-ended questions, language richness and tone. Each teacher gets a 3-minute weekly micro-coaching note on their phone, and directors get a mock-CLASS 'star readiness' report before official visits.
ideas.why_now: On-device diarization and transcription are cheap and good enough. New tax credits and subsidy money (45F at 40-50%, DCFSA to $7,500) are landing in centers in 2026. Child-facing AI is drawing lawsuits, while teacher-facing AI avoids that liability.
ideas.revenue_model: $40-80 per classroom per month, plus an optional success fee (a share of the reimbursement uplift) when the center's tier rises.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Quality is a lever on price, since higher-tier centers earn higher reimbursement, so coaching can be sold as revenue rather than a cost. Putting AI in the adult's ear sidesteps the child-AI liability wave entirely.
ideas.first_30_days: Recruit 3 centers in a state that pays tier bonuses. Record consented lessons on phones and run open-source diarization. Have two ex-CLASS observers score 20 clips to validate the model's ratings. Sell a $500 'star readiness audit' per center, then convert to a monthly plan.

ideas.title: Claims Desk for Government-Paid Childcare
ideas.one_liner: A medical-billing-style revenue-cycle service that turns small providers' attendance sheets into clean subsidy and universal-program claims and advances the cash within 48 hours.
ideas.customer: Family child care homes and one-to-three-site centers in states and cities with subsidy or universal-care programs, such as NYC and New Mexico (the latter from memory).
ideas.problem: As governments become the payer (universal-care promises, 2026 tax credits, tighter CCDF rules), providers face attendance logs, eligibility recertification, claim rejections, 30-60 day payment delays and fraud audits. Margins are thin, payroll is about 70% of cost, and the average worker earns $33,140. Home providers, the fastest-growing segment at +4.3%, have no back office.
ideas.solution: Providers send attendance photos or export from Brightwheel, Procare or Kangarootime. The service validates against each program's rules, fixes errors, submits claims and chases denials. It then offers advances against verified claims, funded by a partner lender. A running library of each state's rejection codes drives the automation.
ideas.why_now: Subsidy-fraud scrutiny and attendance-verification demands rose sharply in winter 2025-26 (from memory, not verified in the brief). Universal or free-care programs are launching and the DCFSA and 45F expansions add spending. Payment-rule changes reward providers who can document cleanly.
ideas.revenue_model: 3-5% of collected subsidy revenue plus a 1.5-3% factoring fee on advances. Payroll-timing savings make it an easy sell.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Healthcare RCM became a giant industry because the payer changed. Childcare is going through the same payer shift with no RCM industry yet. The moat is knowing each state's rejection codes and quirks, which a services-plus-software firm accumulates claim by claim.
ideas.first_30_days: Pick one state with slow, public-rule subsidy payments. Recruit 10 home providers via Facebook provider groups and the local CCR&R. Do the claims by hand with one ops hire and a spreadsheet at 4%. Log every rejection reason. Add advances through a small-business lender partner in month 2.

ideas.title: Age-Tier Compliance for Roblox-Style Creator Studios
ideas.one_liner: Pre-flight scanner and consulting that checks user-generated game experiences against Roblox Kids (<9), Select (9-15) and 16+ tier rules before discovery demotion costs revenue.
ideas.customer: UGC studios and creators earning $200k-$10M a year on Roblox and similar platforms (Fortnite UEFN), plus brand agencies commissioning sponsored experiences.
ideas.problem: Roblox mandated age checks (Jan 2026) and split into Kids, Select and standard tiers in June 2026. Experiences now must match a tier on chat, random-reward purchases, ads, voice and data collection. Misclassified experiences lose tier-based discovery. Indonesia's ban also covers Roblox. Studios don't understand how classification works and brand clients fear child-privacy liability.
ideas.solution: A 'tier lint' tool that combines public metadata with scripted play-throughs to flag features that clash with each tier, gives a fix list (for example, disable free text in Kids, replace loot boxes) and produces a 'brand-safe by tier' report for sponsors. A public changelog tracks platform policy changes.
ideas.why_now: The tier split is only three months old and the rules are still moving. Toy and media brands (Mattel's games push, per the brief) are commissioning kids' UGC experiences, and state attorney-general suits against Roblox (from memory) raise brand caution.
ideas.revenue_model: Subscription at $500-3k a month per studio, plus $5-15k audits for brand-sponsored experiences.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Tiering turns content rating into distribution: the platform's discovery algorithm becomes the regulator, and the UGC studio, not Roblox, eats the cost of getting it wrong. That is a classic compliance-consultancy niche, like Amazon seller-policy work.
ideas.first_30_days: Scrape metadata on the top 500 experiences. Identify about 30 likely mis-tiered ones. Send each studio owner a personalized mini-audit. Sell 10 audits at $1.5k. Start a public policy-change newsletter to build trust.

ideas.title: Friday Programs for Four-Day School Districts
ideas.one_liner: A turnkey 'fifth-day' care and enrichment operator that runs in existing school buildings for districts on four-day weeks, funded by parent fees and vouchers.
ideas.customer: Rural and small-town districts on four-day weeks (hundreds of districts across 20+ states, from memory) and their working parents. Also 21st CCLC and state after-school grant programs.
ideas.problem: Districts adopted four-day weeks to cut costs and recruit teachers. The off day leaves working parents with no care in places where licensed slots are already scarce, so kids stay alone, with grandparents or parents leave jobs. Each district improvises its own Friday program.
ideas.solution: An operating kit: a staffing pool (education majors and retired teachers), background-check pipeline, daily curriculum, parent sign-up and payment, subsidy-voucher billing, insurance and transport. The district provides the building. We run the first sites ourselves, then license the kit for a management fee.
ideas.why_now: ESSER money ended, so more districts are trimming days (from memory). Childcare prices are up 29% since 2020 and rural supply is thin. CCDF rules moving to enrollment-based payment help small operators get paid reliably.
ideas.revenue_model: Parent fee of $35-50 per child per day, with a 15% management fee or per-site licence when franchised to local operators. Voucher billing adds funded slots.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: This desert is a day-of-week desert created by a policy choice, and the most expensive input (the building) is already paid for by taxpayers. That makes the unit economics better than standard childcare.
ideas.first_30_days: Call 20 four-day-week districts in Missouri, Oklahoma and Colorado. Run one paid pilot Friday with 15-25 kids at $40 a day. Recruit staff from the nearest college's education program. Track true margin per child-day and use the data to sell the second district.

ideas.title: Plaintiff-Evidence Pipeline for Kids-Tech Litigation
ideas.one_liner: Software and services that automate platform data requests, device-usage exports and chat-log preservation into court-ready per-plaintiff timelines for firms litigating social media and AI-chatbot harms to minors.
ideas.customer: Plaintiff-side mass-tort firms and litigation funders with hundreds or thousands of minor-plaintiff clients (the social media adolescent-addiction docket, the AI-chatbot wrongful-death wave). Also expert-witness firms.
ideas.problem: Raine v. OpenAI (Aug 2025) opened a wave of suits and the FTC's Sept 2025 6(b) orders raised the stakes. Each plaintiff needs account data from 5-10 platforms, screen-time records and chat exports. Families are non-technical, formats are inconsistent and firms rely on paralegals and spreadsheets.
ideas.solution: A client-facing mobile intake that guides each family through data-export requests (Google Takeout, Meta, TikTok, Snap, ChatGPT and Character.AI exports, Screen Time screenshots via OCR). It adds chain-of-custody hashing, normalizes everything into timelines (late-night usage, DM volume, content categories), redacts third-party minors and outputs expert-ready exhibits.
ideas.why_now: Trials and settlements in 2026 raise the value of well-documented plaintiffs. The volume of AI-chatbot and social-media suits (including Pennsylvania v. Character.AI, May 2026) is growing faster than firms' ops capacity.
ideas.revenue_model: $150-600 per plaintiff processed, or a $2-10k monthly per-firm subscription.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Mass torts are won on aggregate evidence and speed, and the bottleneck is unglamorous plaintiff-level data collection. A picks-and-shovels vendor gets paid whichever side wins.
ideas.first_30_days: Contact 10 boutique mass-tort firms via legal-ops networks. Build a Takeout and Meta-export parser prototype. Charge $250 per plaintiff for a pilot batch of 40. Retain a litigation-support consultant for chain-of-custody rules. Work only through counsel, never soliciting families.

ideas.title: School Deepfake-Nude Incident Response Retainer
ideas.one_liner: A 24/7 retainer that walks school districts through the first 72 hours of an AI-generated nude incident: hash-based takedowns, evidence handling, reporting duties and parent communications.
ideas.customer: School districts, charter networks and independent schools. Channel: school risk pools, cyber and liability insurers and brokers.
ideas.problem: Nudify apps let anyone turn a student photo into sexual imagery. Schools improvise: staff viewing the images can itself be illegal, mandated-reporting and Title IX duties are unclear, and takedowns must be filed on many platforms. The federal TAKE IT DOWN Act (2025) requires platforms to remove reported intimate imagery within 48 hours, with platform compliance due May 2026 (from memory), but victims and schools don't know the process.
ideas.solution: A playbook plus tooling: secure intake that hashes images without staff viewing them (StopNCII and NCMEC Take It Down style), pre-filled takedown requests, a state-by-state legal duty checklist, evidence logs, communication templates for parents and students, and counselor referral. A retained hotline handles live incidents.
ideas.why_now: The TAKE IT DOWN Act's platform obligations kicked in this year, incidents are proliferating, and insurers are re-underwriting districts for cyber and child-safety exposure.
ideas.revenue_model: $3-12k annual retainer per district, per-incident fees, and bundle or referral deals with insurers and school risk pools.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The worst thing a school can do is look at the evidence, so the product is a don't-look-just-hash workflow. Insurers are the channel because one mishandled incident costs far more than the retainer.
ideas.first_30_days: Draft the playbook with a school-law attorney and a former juvenile detective. Pitch 3 school-insurance brokers or state school-board risk pools. Run free tabletop exercises for 5 districts. Convert the best relationship into the first paid retainer.

ideas.title: Contingency-Fee 45F Childcare Tax Credit Shop
ideas.one_liner: An R&D-credit-style boutique that finds, structures and files the newly expanded employer childcare credit (40%, or 50% for small businesses, capped at $500k/$600k) for firms already spending on childcare.
ideas.customer: Mid-market employers (200-5,000 staff) with onsite care or vendor childcare spend: hospitals, manufacturers, universities, credit unions and restaurant chains. Referral channel: their CPA firms.
ideas.problem: The 45F credit was rarely used under its old cap. From January 1, 2026 the credit rose to 40% (50% small business) with $500k ($600k) caps. Eligibility turns on contract structure, licensing, enrollment open to employees and documentation, and it interacts with the new $7,500 DCFSA limit. Generalist CPAs don't know it and CFOs have never claimed it.
ideas.solution: A two-week diagnostic reviews contracts and spend, restructures where needed (for example, reserved-slot agreements with licensed local centers or consortium models), computes the credit and files the forms alongside the client's CPA. Reserved-slot deals also give centers guaranteed enrollment, which helps supply.
ideas.why_now: The changes took effect January 2026, employers set 2027 benefit budgets in Q4 2026, and the first full filing season under the new rules is early 2027.
ideas.revenue_model: Contingency fee of 15-20% of credit claimed (a $250k credit yields $40-50k). Add-on brokerage fee for slot-reservation contracts.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: A $500k cap means the credit can fund a whole classroom's worth of care per employer. The constraint is know-how, not money, and reserved-slot contracts turn a tax credit into childcare supply, a desert fix hidden in the tax code.
ideas.first_30_days: Partner with a tax attorney or CPA who has done R&D or WOTC credits. Build a list of 200 employers advertising childcare benefits (job posts, hospital filings). Publish a two-page 45F guide and a free eligibility screen. Aim for 3 signed contingency engagements.

ideas.title: Age-Signal Rules Engine for App Developers
ideas.one_liner: A 'feature-flag service for minors' law': an SDK that takes the OS or app-store age bracket plus jurisdiction and returns the legally required feature set, with citations and an audit trail.
ideas.customer: Mid-size consumer apps, games and edtech (10-500 staff) with under-18 users, their general counsel, and app agencies. Series A-C startups first.
ideas.problem: Texas app-store age verification (June 2026), Ohio consent (June 2026), Florida under-14 ban, California's OS age-attestation law, the UK regime, and bans in Australia, Brazil, Indonesia and Malaysia each define brackets and required behavior differently. Engineers hard-code rules and rules change monthly. Fines are large.
ideas.solution: A versioned policy graph maintained by lawyers plus LLM change tracking. The SDK returns flags for chat, DMs, push timing, ads, purchases and recommendation feeds per bracket and jurisdiction. It integrates with OS age-range signals and third-party verifiers and logs which rule applied when, for regulators.
ideas.why_now: For the first time OS and app stores hand developers an age signal (California signed Oct 2025; Apple and Google age-range APIs, from memory), but nobody says what to do with it. The 'policy ratchet' means fragmentation will grow.
ideas.revenue_model: $500-5k a month by MAU tier, plus one-time compliance-matrix audits at $3-6k.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Age-verification vendors sell the signal, and nobody sells the decision: the legal mapping from signal to product behavior. That mapping is the durable moat because laws keep diverging.
ideas.first_30_days: Publish a public 8-jurisdiction by 5-feature matrix. Run a newsletter around it. Sell 5 compliance-matrix audits at $4k to game and app teams. Wrap the logic into an SDK by month 3.

ideas.title: UL for Talking Toys: Behavioral Safety Lab
ideas.one_liner: An independent lab that red-teams AI toys and kid-facing companion gadgets with child personas, then sells scorecards and a 'passed' seal to brands and retailers.
ideas.customer: AI-toy brands and ODMs launching in the US, licensors of kids' IP, and big-box and online retailers' product-safety and legal teams, plus toy-industry insurers.
ideas.problem: Physical toy labs test lead and choking hazards but nobody tests what a toy says across a 200-turn conversation, whether guardrails drift, where audio goes, or whether privacy claims are true. Late-2025 consumer testing reportedly found AI toys giving inappropriate content (not verified in the brief). Retailers carry the liability, and the FTC's 6(b) inquiry, SB 243 and the amended COPPA rule raise the stakes.
ideas.solution: A standard suite of about 300 child-persona conversations (ages 4-12, varied accents), child-style jailbreak probing, sensitive-topic sweeps, long-horizon persona drift, network capture of data flows and retention, and verification of COPPA claims. Deliverables are a scorecard, fix list, re-test and a versioned seal retailers can require.
ideas.why_now: Holiday 2026 is the first mass AI-toy season (Mattel-OpenAI partnership, from memory; Character.AI's under-18 exit), and retailers' legal teams need evidence by Q4. The buying window is right now.
ideas.revenue_model: $12-40k per product per version, annual retainers for brands, and seal licensing fees.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Retailers, not parents, are the choke point, and they buy assurance rather than products. The test is dynamic (behavior over time) rather than static (materials), which makes it a new category of lab created by regulators' fear.
ideas.first_30_days: Buy 10 AI toys and gadgets (about $1.5k) and publish a public holiday AI-toy behavior report with methodology. Send private reports to 5 retailer compliance heads and 10 brands. Offer paid re-tests to any brand that fails.

ideas.title: Trust-Fund Compliance for Family Vloggers
ideas.one_liner: A minutes-on-screen tracker and escrow tool that computes, sets aside and documents the trust share owed to kids who appear in monetized family channels.
ideas.customer: Family channel operators on YouTube, TikTok and Instagram earning $50k+ a year, influencer agencies and MCNs, and brands and payment processors that want a 'clean hands' certificate.
ideas.problem: Several states have passed laws on minors in monetized content: Illinois (2024) requires a trust share by on-screen time, Minnesota (2025) restricts under-14 content creation for pay, and California extended Coogan-style protections (details from memory). Parents compute set-asides by hand. Brands and platforms are exposed, and grown kids and documentaries are fueling backlash.
ideas.solution: The tool ingests channel data, uses vision models to measure each child's on-screen minutes per video, computes the state-specific set-aside, generates records and moves funds into a custodial trust, UTMA or custodial investment account. It also keeps consent and deletion logs and issues brand-facing compliance certificates.
ideas.why_now: The state laws took effect in 2024-25, public scrutiny of family-vlogging is at a high, and a new custodial-account channel (Trump Accounts, opened July 2026, per the brief) gives set-asides a natural home.
ideas.revenue_model: $99-499 a month per channel or about 1% of earnings, plus per-campaign brand compliance certificates.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The real buyers are brands and platforms that need a clean-hands certificate, and creators who need to avoid legal exposure. It works like marketplace sales-tax automation, and the child is the beneficiary, not the customer.
ideas.first_30_days: Ship a free on-screen-minutes calculator. DM 100 family channels with 50k-2M subscribers. Sell a $299 compliance setup with an attorney-reviewed template. Approach 3 influencer agencies for a group deal.

ideas.title: Youth-Slang Drift API for Safety Teams
ideas.one_liner: A continuously updated, human-verified lexicon and drift detector for Gen Alpha and teen slang, coded risk terms and grooming language, sold as an API to moderation and school-safety teams.
ideas.customer: Trust-and-safety teams at game and social platforms, K-12 student-monitoring vendors, school-safety directors, and moderation stacks inside AI toys and companions.
ideas.problem: Youth language shifts every few months. Classifiers trained on last year's data misread banter and miss coded terms for sextortion, self-harm and grooming. School monitors bury counselors in false alerts. As bans push kids into private chats and games, moderation teams are older and further from the language.
ideas.solution: A lexicon with context tags (benign, hazard, coded-risk; severity; platform of origin; age range), plus alerts when a term's usage or meaning shifts, delivered via API and a weekly briefing. It is built with a paid panel of consented 16-19-year-old language scouts (parental consent where needed) and linguists.
ideas.why_now: Age-gated platform tiers, bans and duty-of-care laws raise the cost of missed threats. Moderation is now LLM-based and needs fresh context that models lack. Volume and speed of Gen Alpha slang keep growing.
ideas.revenue_model: $2-15k a month per platform or vendor for API and briefings, plus custom lexicon builds.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: LLMs know last year's slang, so freshness is a data-supply problem. The moat is the paid youth panel and labeling process, not the model.
ideas.first_30_days: Recruit 10 teens (with parental consent) and 3 linguists. Publish a free monthly 'Gen Alpha threat lexicon' for trust-and-safety newsletters. Land 2 design partners, one school-monitoring vendor and one kids' game, at $1k a month each.

ideas.title: Toddler Talk: Voice-Based Developmental Screening
ideas.one_liner: A phone-recorded three-minute parent-child talk sample plus automated screening workflow that helps pediatric practices catch speech and developmental delays earlier and capture reimbursement.
ideas.customer: Pediatric practices and health systems (developmental screening is billable under CPT 96110), Early Intervention programs and Medicaid managed care plans.
ideas.problem: Speech-language delay is a very common developmental issue, but screening relies on parent questionnaires with modest sensitivity, practices under-screen and Early Intervention waitlists are long. Kids are referred late.
ideas.solution: Phase 1 (no diagnostic claims) is a text-based well-visit screening workflow that increases completion and billing capture and collects consented audio. Phase 2 adds speech models that estimate vocabulary diversity, word combinations and turn-taking latency, giving clinicians a triage report. Phase 3 is a validated FDA pathway.
ideas.why_now: Speech models now handle child speech far better than before. Developmental screening is a CMS Child Core Set quality measure (from memory), so Medicaid plans pay for completion. Multimodal models make sample-based scoring feasible.
ideas.revenue_model: Per-screen fee or per-provider subscription ($200-500 a month), plus quality-improvement contracts with Medicaid plans, and later a per-report fee.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Parents already record toddlers constantly. The bottleneck is not detection technology but screening completion and triage, so the winning move is to attach to the reimbursed screening code and Medicaid quality measures first and upgrade the signal later.
ideas.first_30_days: Partner with 2 independent pediatric practices through a developmental-behavioral pediatrician advisor. Run a 60-day free text-intake screening pilot. Capture consented audio for retrospective validation. Pitch one Medicaid plan's quality team on completion-rate lift.

ideas.title: Verified-Guardian Credential Built on Childcare Centers
ideas.one_liner: Start as a custody-aware pickup and consent app for childcare centers, then turn those institutions into issuers of privacy-preserving 'verified parent of a child aged X' tokens that apps pay for.
ideas.customer: First: childcare centers, camps and youth orgs (SaaS at $50-150 per site per month). Later: app stores, game studios and platforms (per-attestation fees), and state agencies.
ideas.problem: Parental-consent laws (Ohio, Florida, Texas and others) need a verified parent, but credit-card or ID checks prove adulthood, not parenthood. OS vendors will supply age attestation but not guardian relationships. Meanwhile childcare centers and schools already verify guardian-child relationships, custody orders and authorized pickup, and that verification is not reusable.
ideas.solution: Phase 1 is a check-in and pickup app with ID and liveness verification for guardians, custody-order parsing, an authorized pickup list, and e-consent for photos, trips and immunizations. Phase 2 lets the center vouch, through zero-knowledge or selective-disclosure tokens, that an adult is a verified guardian of a child in an age band, without revealing identities to apps.
